# Māgaṇḍiya Sutta (MN 75 (PTS MN i 501))

**ID:** MN 75 (PTS MN i 501)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Māgaṇḍiya Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** With Māgaṇḍiya
**PTS:** MN i 501

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Māgaṇḍiya Sutta* (MN 75) is a discourse in the *Majjhimanikāya* recording an encounter between the Buddha and the wanderer (*paribbājaka*) Māgaṇḍiya [Hazra 1994; Onians 2002]. Māgaṇḍiya accuses the Buddha of being a "destroyer of life/growth" (*bhūnahu*) or repressionist due to his teachings against sensory gratification [Hazra 1994; Eifring 2014; Onians 2002]. The Buddha rejects this label and recounts his pre-awakening youth living in luxurious palaces surrounded by sensory entertainments, explaining that he later saw the gratification, danger, and escape regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure and renounced them [Bareau; Anālayo 2017]. Through this abandonment, he attained an inner peace and a higher happiness far surpassing worldly pleasures [Bareau; Anālayo 2017].

A focal point of the sutta is its criticism of sensual desires through vivid similes, most notably that of a leper [Goodman 2009; Davis and Flanagan; Anālayo 2014]. Indulging in sensual pleasures is compared to a leper scratching raw wounds and cauterizing them over hot coals: though providing momentary relief, the scratching and burning only worsen the affliction [Goodman 2009; Davis and Flanagan; Eifring 2014; Anālayo 2014; Anālayo 2018]. Once cured of leprosy, a person views that fire with revulsion and would resist being dragged to it; similarly, one who has transcended sensual lust does not envy those indulging in worldly pleasures [Goodman 2009; Davis and Flanagan; Anālayo 2014]. The discourse also touches upon the affective structure of feelings, emphasizing that pleasant, painful, and neutral feelings cannot be experienced at the same time [Anālayo 2014].

 DharmaNexus also detects textual reuse in the Tibetan *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* (D 6) and the *Avadānaśataka* (D 343), as well as the Sanskrit *Lalitavistara* [DharmaNexus]. Canonical verse parallels correspond to *Dhammapada* 204, the Gāndhārī and Patna Dharmapadas, and the *Udānavarga* (chapter 26), and the sutta is discussed in the *Milindapañha* (Mil 6.3.9). Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus records extensive text reuse across 174 texts, sharing long passages especially with the *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), and *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7) [DharmaNexus].
